name: DT 285
location_notes:
Necropolis 200m south of racetrack, either deposited into inhumation burials or rolled up and inserted into libation tubes. (Heintz 1998)
Necropolis along the road connecting Sousse and Kairouan on the southern side of the road, some 500 meters away from the “Camp des Tirailleurs” and 300 meters away from the Punic necropolis.(Sánchez 2023)

Audollent: His research focused primarily on the region
located south of the road [Kairouan versus], approximately 500 meters from the Tirailleurs Camp, and 300 meters from the boundary of the Punic necropolis; and there, in cremation tombs, he collected a number of magical tablets; only one of them is of the type of love spells; the
others relate to racing horses.... They all come from two tombs: the first contained six (only five could be unrolled), the second five, rolled up according to custom.

We possess fourteen lead plates; two of them
were open, the other twelve rolled up. The
lead is generally so oxidized that, despite all precautions, it is impossible to open them without breaking them. The two plates found open had a hole made by a large nail, still attached to the plate, as if someone had tried to hold them pressed against one of the faces of the tomb.

I had eleven, not fourteen, leaden volumes at hand, which I mentioned above, and I saw no love ones.

We have no precise data on the age of these tombs. “They contained,” wrote General Goetschy to me, “no funerary furnishings. According to the lamps found in the tombs immediately adjacent to the lead-lined tombs, I suppose that those containing the first seven were from the beginning of the 1st century, and those containing the last five from the end of that same century or the beginning of the 11th.” "Since we cannot, for various reasons, attribute the five imprecations cited above (276-280) to the end of the 2nd century or rather to the 3rd century, we must conclude that the tombs in question, if they truly date from the 1st century, had already existed for a long time when the idea arose to use them for magical operations."

In Hadrumetum, in the cemetery next to the hippodrome, a 2nd century curse
tablet was found, on which a drawing of a horse could be seen.7 The horse’s
name (Laureatus) was also written into the drawing. According to Faraone, the
maker of the tablet may have drawn only the head of the horse, or perhaps the
whole animal, but the layout of the tablet did not allow space larger than 25
Greek letters wide. The tablet was published by A. Audollent, but he did not attach
a drawing, and unfortunately we cannot find the drawing of this tablet
among the documents in his bequest. This complex curse inscription included
voces magicae, names of demons and divinities, charaktēres and a drawing, too (nemeth cursed horses)

notes_on_image:
Sichet: Notes

A/ As for Villefosse, Choppard, Hannezo, and Wuensch, it is a rooster-headed genie Audollent disagrees and believes it to be a human head with a beard surmounted by a rooster's comb. Having been unable to see for myself what it was, I am only reporting two hypotheses here. But this demon is still the subject of several controversies: regarding its identification, Maspéro thinks this demon belongs to the astronomical decans (cf. Audollent, DT. no. 15, 8, p. 25), Gauckler calls it a set (Cat. Alaoui, H, 31-33). As for its attributes, a flaming torch occupies its left hand, and a vase, its right, but Villefosse sees it as a lit incense burner supported by a long stem, Choppard and Hannezo see it as a torch; Wuensch sees it as a torch, and Audollent does not offer an opinion. The difficulty of reaching a consensus on a single representation is clear. The one thing we are certain of is that he is standing on a boat. The names inscribed in the boat do not refer to the demon; they are those of the bewitched horses. We have already seen Oceanum in tablet nos. 54, 58, 63 (DT. 275, 16/279, 14/284, 12). On the demon's chest, Audollent thought it should read Daitmo Arditto, but later studies have shown that it is Baitmo Arbitto, a transcription of the Hebrew.

The iconographic model of a figure standing on a ship without a mast can be traced back to Isis Pelagia, who was also depicted in Roman coinage.33 According to R. Gordon, the ship stands for the unstoppable power of fate but we can also think of it as a means of transport between our world and the otherworld, similar to the vessel of Charon. If the object in its left hand is really an urn, then Baitmo is probably the nekydaimon from the grave where the lamella was buried, who was addressed with the following words in DTAud 286: Adiuro te demon quicunque es et demando tibi… (nemeth 2013)

Opisthograph tablet, high m. 0.11, wide m. 0.08 — 0.09, third p. Chr. n. century written, found in the tomb of a certain "untimely dead" (the greek word) (cf. Cagnat, Sav., p. 264)

Sichet Commentary
The charioteers Clarus, Felix, Primulus, and Romanus are bewitched; they belong to the green and white factions, as do their horses.
This tablet consists, on one side, of the adjuration against the elements mentioned above and is accompanied, as seen in Figure 4, by the representation of a rooster-headed genie (?) standing on a boat and holding a torch.
In addition to the demons that we will later encounter in Cuigeu... We find a first mention of the deus pelagicus, which we will also see again.
Between the fifth and sixth lines of the first face (that of the invocation), there is, according to observers, a hole probably made by the nail that was used to fix the lead sheet inside the tomb.

in 1893 bulletin archaeologique BCTH - pg 194
The description of the principal hypogea has already been given in previous reports; the only ones not mentioned are either of no interest, having been violated long ago, or collapsed, or in such a poor state of preservation that it did not seem prudent to conduct any research there.

The grouped tombs generally take the form of square cippi and sometimes of tombs, called coffin tombs, of a semi-cylindrical shape.

We found in the same place sixteen square cippi, very closely spaced, which provided the lead tablets (tabellae devotionis) described later. These cippi closely resemble those discovered in 1888 in the Roman cemetery of Carthage; their average dimensions are 1.50 meters high and 0.95 meters wide; they are made of masonry, and their exterior, outside the original natural ground level, is smooth, stuccoed, and sometimes ornamented. Inside the cippus, embedded in the masonry, is a bone container. This container may be either a two-handled amphora, often pierced with a hole in the lower part, or a spherical vessel similar to the Arabic keskess, pierced with holes

These two types of containers hold calcined bones; in the spherical vessel, one sometimes finds, lying flat on the bones or rolled on a bone, a lead tabella devotionis.

Among the tombs of the Roman cemetery along the road leading to Kairouan, excavated at various times, all the Hadrumetine tablets were unearthed (268-298). We are only taught about most of them; the invention of some is also narrated below on p. 361 and 378.

“His research focused primarily on the region south of the road [Kairouan versus], approximately 500 meters from the Tirailleurs Camp, and 300 meters from the edge of the Punic necropolis. There, in cremation tombs, he collected a number of magical tablets; only one of them is of the type used for love spells; the others relate to racing horses… They all come from two tombs: the first contained six (only five could be unrolled), the second five, rolled up according to custom.”

Pauca addidit Goetschy (Archaeological Bulletin, 1903, p. 166):

“We possess fourteen lead tablets; two of them were open, the other twelve rolled up.” The lead is generally so oxidized that, despite all precautions, it is impossible to open them without breaking them. The two plates found open were pierced by a large nail, still adhered to the plate, as if someone had wanted to hold them against one of the faces of the tomb. »

Haec tandem e Cagnati commentatione (Sav., p. 264) excer
pere iuvat: “We have no precise data on the age of these tombs. “They contained,” writes General Goetschy to me, “no funerary furnishings. According to the lamps found in the tombs immediately adjacent to the lead-slab tombs, I suppose that those containing the first seven were from the beginning of the 1st century, and those containing the last five were from the end of that same century or the beginning of the 11th.” “Since we cannot, for various reasons, attribute the five imprecations cited above (276-280) to anything other than the end of the 2nd century or rather to the 3rd century, we must conclude that the tombs in question, if they truly date from the 1st century, had already existed for a long time when the idea arose to use them for magical operations.”

I conjure you, demon, whoever you may be, and I ask you, this day, this hour, this moment, that Advocata be tortured by him who took your life, god of the sea, of the air. I conjure you to mistreat these horses... I entrust them to you.

(Sichet 2000)
This tablet relates, through formulas similar to those of the defixiones concerning circus horses, to Advocata. But Audollent speaks of her as Advocata, so it is more likely a woman than a circus charioteer

Gauckler calls Set, the demon god who is depicted on this tablet. However, he is called Iao in the earlier tablets
circus/charioteers

(Audollent)
Legi et descripsi; cf. Cat. Alaoui, H, 32, with a zincotype image in tab. XXVIII.

An opisthographical tablet, 0.11 m high and 0.088 m wide, was found with the preceding ones.

A demon sitting on a cement structure outlined with oblique lines, holding a whip in his left hand. Before the demon's feet, a human protome.

Because of the similarity of the formulas between the defixations that pertain to circus horses, I have reported this, although Advocata (6 4), if I read it correctly, designates a woman rather than a driver. Gaucklero decided to call the figured demon god Set (Cat. Alaoui).

name: DT 293
location_notes:
Necropolis 200m south of racetrack, either deposited into inhumation burials or rolled up and inserted into libation tubes. (Heintz 1998)
Necropolis along the road connecting Sousse and Kairouan on the southern side of the road, some 500 meters away from the “Camp des Tirailleurs” and 300 meters away from the Punic necropolis.(Sánchez 2023)

Audollent: His research focused primarily on the region
located south of the road [Kairouan versus], approximately 500 meters from the Tirailleurs Camp, and 300 meters from the boundary of the Punic necropolis; and there, in cremation tombs, he collected a number of magical tablets; only one of them is of the type of love spells; the
others relate to racing horses.... They all come from two tombs: the first contained six (only five could be unrolled), the second five, rolled up according to custom.

We possess fourteen lead plates; two of them
were open, the other twelve rolled up. The
lead is generally so oxidized that, despite all precautions, it is impossible to open them without breaking them. The two plates found open had a hole made by a large nail, still attached to the plate, as if someone had tried to hold them pressed against one of the faces of the tomb.

I had eleven, not fourteen, leaden volumes at hand, which I mentioned above, and I saw no love ones.

We have no precise data on the age of these tombs. “They contained,” wrote General Goetschy to me, “no funerary furnishings. According to the lamps found in the tombs immediately adjacent to the lead-lined tombs, I suppose that those containing the first seven were from the beginning of the 1st century, and those containing the last five from the end of that same century or the beginning of the 11th.” "Since we cannot, for various reasons, attribute the five imprecations cited above (276-280) to the end of the 2nd century or rather to the 3rd century, we must conclude that the tombs in question, if they truly date from the 1st century, had already existed for a long time when the idea arose to use them for magical operations."

Les vestiges antiques de la ville d’Hadrumetum, d’après L. Maurin, « L’épitaphe de Claudius Chrestus », Africa 23, 2013.

translation:
sichet
A/ Up to line 6, these are magical formulas. Then: I conjure you, demon, whoever you may be, and I ask you this day, this hour, this moment, to torture this one, this day, I conjure you by him who took your life, the god of the sea, of the air, the highest god, Iaô (Greek letters follow). Reversed, it reads: May Lynceus and Peciolus be broken

B/ I conjure you, demon, whoever you may be, and I ask you this day, this hour, this moment, let him be tortured. I conjure you by him who took your life, the god of the sea, of the air, the most high god Lao (Greek letters follow). Only one name comes after, Lynceus
notes:
Sichet 2000:
Notes:

A/ Lines 2 and 20: Audollent informs us that the magic word anox can be read on a silver tablet held by the Kircheriano Museum (cf. Ruggiero, Cataloguó del Museo Kircheriano, 1878, p. 81, n. 200). It is also found on tablet no. 74 (DT, no. 295, 5).

Lines 7 and 11: It should be corrected to dajemon.

Line 8: Anc should be replaced by hac.

Line 10: Vite is substituted for vitfaje.

B/ Lines 3-4: Hanc and (h)oc should be restored.

Commentary:

The name Lynceus is given for the first time in A 15; he is bewitched. He reappears in B 12, so that the demons may manifest themselves against him.

This inscription, like some of the previous ones, is also used to bewitch circus horses. Tablet no. 68 (DT. no. 289, all) designates a horse named Lynceus like this one, but we also find here a horse named Peciolus, which we will find again, in line 20, of the following tablet, Here again, lines 12-13 of A and 10-11 of B are a transcription ofHebrew.
